title: Looking After Animals
hint: Feed, milk, graze, shear, muck out; trough, hay and straw; routines with always/usually; let them out, bring them in
why: farm animals need care every single day, in every kind of weather. The words for these jobs are useful on a farm visit, in stories and in the news, and talking about daily routines (She always feeds the calves first) is one of the most common things we do in English.
know: the daily jobs: feed, water, milk, graze, groom, shear, muck out
things on the farm: trough, hay, straw, feed, milking parlour, sheepdog, vet
phrasal verbs: let out, bring in, round up, check on
understand: where adverbs of frequency go: She always feeds the calves but The calves are always hungry
why we say let them out, not let out them
able: describe a farmer's daily routine, or your own routine with a pet
say how often things happen on a farm
talk about how animals should be looked after
mistakes: She feeds always the calves first.
The cows always are hungry in the morning.
The cows are always hungry in the morning.
The farmer milks the cows two times in a day.
The farmer milks the cows twice a day.
We put clean hay on the floor for them to sleep on.
We put clean straw on the floor. (hay is food)
The cow gave birth to a calf yesterday night.
The cow gave birth to a calf last night. / The cow calved last night.
warmup: Do you have a pet, or did you have one as a child? Who looked after it?
What do you think a dairy farmer does every day? What time does the day start?
Which animal job would you like to try: milking a cow, feeding lambs or brushing a horse? Which would you hate?

rows: give food to an animal (fed, fed)
give water to an animal or plant
take milk from a cow, goat or sheep
The cows are milked twice a day.
The sheep graze on the hills all summer.
brush and clean an animal's coat
She grooms her horse after every ride.
cut the wool off a sheep (sheared, shorn)
clean the dirty straw out of a stable or shed
I muck out the stable every morning.

vocab.note: These phrasal verbs can be split. With a noun, both orders are fine: let the hens out or let out the hens. With a pronoun (it, them), the pronoun must go in the middle: let them out, never let out them.
rows: open the door so animals can go outside
Let the hens out at eight. Let them out at eight.
bring animals inside, into a building
Bring the sheep in before the storm.
bring animals together into one group or place
The dog rounds them up in ten minutes.
close the door so animals stay inside
Shut the chickens in at night, because of the foxes.
go and see if an animal is OK (not separable)
I check on the new calf every two hours.
a long open container for animals' food or water
hay = dried grass, food; straw = dry stems, bedding
food for animals (uncountable): a bag of feed
the building where cows are milked (US parlor)
a dog trained to move sheep
the weeks in spring when the lambs are born
verbs: give birth to a calf, a lamb, a foal: The cow calved last night.

vocab.note: Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb (She always feeds them) but after be (They are always hungry). Longer phrases go at the end: twice a day, every morning, once a week.
rows: The cows always come to the gate at milking time.
We usually shear the sheep in June.
The vet often visits in lambing season.
A dairy farmer never has a day off.

say: trough rhymes with off (/trɒf/); shear sounds like sheer; shorn rhymes with born; calve has a silent l; muck rhymes with duck.

exercises.title: Reading
exercises.text:
My week as a farm volunteer: Monday

I arrived at Hillside Farm in Nova Scotia last night, and today I started work at half past five! The cows are always milked first. They walk into the milking parlour on their own, because they know the routine. While Jenna milked them, I fed the calves with big bottles of warm milk. They pushed me so hard that I nearly fell over.

After breakfast we let the cows out into the field to graze. Then I mucked out the calf shed. It's a dirty job, but the clean straw smells lovely. Jenna checks the water troughs twice a day, because a cow can drink up to a hundred litres of water on a hot day.

In the afternoon the vet came to see a cow that was limping. Luckily it was only a small stone in her foot.

At six o'clock the cows were milked again, and then Rex, the old sheepdog, helped us round up the sheep and bring them in for the night. I was in bed by nine. I'm tired, but I've never been happier.
exercises.intro: Read the diary. Then type the missing word from the text, and press Check.

items.ask: What time did the writer start work?
items.why: Paragraph 1: 'today I started work at half past five!'

items.ask: What did the writer feed the calves with?
items.why: Paragraph 1: 'I fed the calves with big bottles of warm milk.'

items.ask: How much water can a cow drink on a hot day?
items.why: Paragraph 2: 'a cow can drink up to a hundred litres of water on a hot day'.

items.pre: To see a cow that was
items.why: Paragraph 3: 'the vet came to see a cow that was limping'.

items.ask: Who helped round up the sheep?
items.why: Paragraph 4: 'Rex, the old sheepdog, helped us round up the sheep'.

exercises.title: Speaking
items: Imagine a day on a dairy farm. What does the farmer do in the morning, the afternoon and the evening? Use always, usually, never.
Have you ever looked after an animal (a pet, a neighbour's dog, a farm animal)? What did you do every day?
Would you like to be a farm volunteer for a week? Which jobs would you enjoy, and which would you avoid?
How should farm animals be looked after? Is it important to you that animals live outside and graze?

parts.rule:
Watch out

  • out: from inside to outside, or cleaning something completely: let the hens out, muck out the shed
  • in: from outside to inside: bring the sheep in, shut the hens in
  • up: together, or completely: round up the cattle, fill up the trough
parts.intro: Which word completes each phrase? Sort them.

chips.why: Let out = open the door so the animals can go outside.
Muck out = clean all the dirty straw out of a stable or shed.

chips.t: turn the horses ___ into the field
chips.why: Turn out = put animals outside in a field to graze.
Bring in = bring animals inside, into a building.

chips.t: shut the chickens ___ for the night
chips.why: Shut in = close the door so the animals stay inside.
Come in = come inside: Come in out of the rain!
Round up = bring animals together into one group or place.
Fill up = fill something completely: fill up the trough with water.
Pick up = take something from the ground or a surface: pick up the eggs.
Clean up = make a place completely clean and tidy.

items.q: Please let out them before nine.
items.why: With a pronoun, it goes in the middle of the phrasal verb: let them out.

items.q: She feeds always the pigs at seven.
items.why: Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb: She always feeds the pigs.

items.q: The sheep are never left alone during lambing season.
items.why: Correct: with be, the adverb goes after it: are never left.

items.q: The cows is milked twice a day.
items.why: Cows is plural, so use are: The cows are milked twice a day.

items.q: We put clean hay on the floor for the horses to sleep on.
items.why: Animals sleep on straw. Hay is food.

teacher.purpose: give general learners the words for looking after farm animals (feed, milk, graze, groom, shear, muck out), the things they use (trough, hay, straw, feed, milking parlour), farm phrasal verbs (let out, bring in, round up, check on) and routine language: adverbs of frequency and where they go.
teacher.before: find a photo of a milking parlour, a sheep being shorn and a sheepdog at work. Optional: a short sheepdog trial video (search “sheepdog trial”). Students love it, and it shows round up and bring in perfectly.
plan: The three warm-up questions. If the student has a pet, use it for routine language straight away: “How often do you feed it?”

Daily jobs first, with photos or mime (milking, brushing, shearing). Then the phrasal verbs: show the pronoun rule on the board: let the hens out / let them out / let out them. Then the frequency box.
Matching, then routines and phrasal verbs. In Exercise 2, ask the student to explain each adverb position: before the verb, after be.
Do one together and set the other for home.

The volunteer's diary. First ask: “Would you like Jenna's job?” Then the questions. Then ask the student to retell the day in the present simple as Jenna's routine: She always milks the cows first ...
Questions 1 and 2 are the core. Push for a frequency word in every sentence, and at least two phrasal verbs.
Exercise 7 Part A together; Part B at home.
pron: trough /trɒf/ (North American /trɔːf/): rhymes with off. Another -ough word, like plough in Lesson 4, but a different sound.
shear /ʃɪə/ sounds like sheer; shorn /ʃɔːn/ rhymes with born. Contrast with share /ʃeə/.
muck /mʌk/ rhymes with duck. Watch the vowel: not mock.
Phrasal verbs are stressed on the particle: let them OUT, bring them IN, round them UP.
mistakes: Adverb position: many languages put the adverb after the verb (She feeds always). Rule: before the main verb, after be. Sometimes can also go at the start.
Pronouns with phrasal verbs: let them out, not let out them. But check on does not split: check on them.
hay vs straw (from Lesson 4): hay is food, straw is bedding. feed is also a noun for animal food and is uncountable: a bag of feed, not a feed.
two times in a day: say twice a day, three times a week, once a month. No in.
yesterday night: say last night. Very common from Spanish, French and Chinese speakers.
Birth verbs: a cow calves, a ewe lambs, a mare foals. In general English: gives birth to, or a calf was born. Watch for was borned or is born yesterday.
vet: in North America also veterinarian; in the UK veterinary surgeon. Vet also means a military veteran in North America.
uk_us: Canada uses the British spelling, parlour.
Border collies are the classic sheepdog breed.
adapt: Six jobs (feed, milk, graze, groom, shear, muck out), the trough and hay/straw, and three phrasal verbs (let out, bring in, round up). Adverbs: always, usually, sometimes, never.
All words; add fodder, bedding, livestock auction, to tag, to vaccinate, to wean, and phrasal verbs turn out, see to, put down (also: end an animal's life).
Describe a farmer's day, or your own routine with a pet, using frequency words.
Discuss animal welfare: indoor vs outdoor farming, free-range labels, what makes a good life for a farm animal.
prompts: A day on a dairy farm. Follow up: “What does she do first?” “How often are the cows milked?” “Does she ever have a day off?” Listen for adverb position.
Looking after an animal. Follow up: “Who took it for walks?” “What did you do when it was ill?” Good for past routines too.
A week as a volunteer. Follow up: “What time would you get up?” “Would you muck out the stables?” Encourage reasons with because and so.

How animals should be looked after. A B2 stretch: opinions with I think they should ... Follow up: “Would you pay more for milk from cows that graze outside?” This leads into Lesson 6 (free-range, organic).

bank.q: My uncle ___ up at five, even on Sundays.
bank.why: Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb: He always gets up at five.

bank.q: The goats ___ hungry when we arrive.
bank.why: With be, the adverb goes after it: The goats are usually hungry.

bank.q: Could you let the ducks ___ onto the pond?
bank.why: Let out = open the door so the animals can go outside.

bank.q: The cows are ___ twice a day, at six and at five.
bank.why: Cows are milked: the milk is taken from them, usually twice a day.

bank.q: Put fresh ___ down in the stable. The horses need a clean bed.
bank.why: Straw is bedding: animals sleep on it. Hay and feed are food.

bank.q: A storm is coming. Let's bring the horses ___.
bank.why: Bring in = bring animals inside, into a building.

bank.q: The sheep ___ on the hills from May to October.
bank.why: Graze = eat grass in a field or on hills.

bank.q: The farmer gets up every two hours in the night to ___ the new lambs.
bank.why: Check on = go and see if someone or something is OK.

bank.q: A doctor for animals is called a ___.
bank.why: A vet (veterinarian) is a doctor for animals.

bank.q: Our mare ___ last spring, and now we have a beautiful young horse.
bank.why: Foal = give birth to a foal (a young horse). Past: foaled.

bank.q: The pigs drink from a long metal ___ in the yard.
bank.why: A trough is a long open container for animals' food or water.

bank.q: Every morning I muck ___ the stable and put down clean straw.
bank.why: Muck out = clean the dirty straw out of a stable or shed.

bank.q: The sheep were ___ last week, so now they look very thin.
bank.why: Shear, sheared, shorn: the wool was cut off. Shorn is the usual past participle.

bank.q: The dog rounded up them very quickly.
bank.why: With a pronoun, it goes in the middle: rounded them up.

bank.q: We feed the chickens two times in a day.
bank.why: Say twice a day: no in. Also once a week, three times a month.

bank.q: Hens usually lay their eggs in the morning.
bank.why: Correct: usually goes before the main verb lay.

bank.q: She grooms her horse after every ride.
bank.why: Correct: groom = brush and clean a horse's coat.

bank.a: How often does the vet visit the farm?
bank.why: Question: How often + does + subject + verb?

bank.a: We never leave the gate open at night.
bank.why: Never goes before the main verb: We never leave the gate open.

bank.a: Shut them in before the foxes come.
bank.why: With a pronoun, it goes in the middle: shut them in.
